name: Marrakech
tagline: Spice-scented souks, riad courtyards and Atlas-framed sunsets
description:
Marrakech ambushes the senses in the best possible way. Inside the ochre ramparts of the medina, donkey carts squeeze past scooters in lanes barely wider than your shoulders, the air smells of cedar shavings, cumin and orange blossom, and every studded doorway hides a courtyard riad or a workshop of coppersmiths hammering in rhythm. At dusk, Jemaa el-Fnaa becomes the world's greatest open-air stage, with storytellers, Gnawa musicians and smoking grill stalls packed shoulder to shoulder.

Beyond the chaos lies astonishing craftsmanship: carved cedar and zellige tilework in the Bahia Palace, the jewel-box courtyard of the Ben Youssef Madrasa, and the electric-blue calm of the Majorelle Garden. Modern Gueliz adds galleries, rooftop bars and French-accented cafés.

Come with patience and a sense of humour — haggling is a sport, getting lost is guaranteed and mint tea is the answer to most questions. When the medina gets too much, the snow-streaked High Atlas is barely an hour away, with Berber villages, waterfalls and walnut groves in the Ourika Valley.

safety.notes: Serious crime against tourists is uncommon, but expect persistent touts and self-appointed 'guides' in the medina — a firm, friendly 'la, shukran' works. Keep phones and bags on the wall side of lanes where scooters zip past.

tipping: Leave about 10% in sit-down restaurants, and keep 10–20 DH coins handy for porters, parking attendants, hammam staff and any performer you photograph.
gettingAround: The medina is best explored on foot with an offline map; petit taxis are cheap if you insist on the meter or agree the fare first, and the airport is only about 15 minutes from the centre.
tips: Cars can't enter most medina lanes, so ask your riad to meet you at the nearest taxi drop-off — hunting for it alone on arrival night is a rite of passage worth skipping.
Start haggling at around a third to half of the first price, keep it light-hearted, and only name a number you're genuinely willing to pay.
Politely ignore anyone insisting a street is 'closed' or offering to lead you to the tanneries — it's a well-worn detour to a commission shop.
Carry small notes and coins; many souk stalls and taxis don't take cards and rarely have change for a 200 DH note.
Book a timed Majorelle Garden ticket online for the first slot of the day; by late morning the queues and crowds build fast.
During Ramadan many cafés close by day and the pace slows, but evenings after iftar are festive — eat and drink discreetly in public during daylight.
etiquette: Dress modestly in the medina — covering shoulders and knees earns more respect and noticeably less hassle.
Non-Muslims can't enter most active mosques, including the Koutoubia, so admire the architecture from outside.
Ask before photographing people, and expect to tip performers, water sellers and snake charmers in Jemaa el-Fnaa if you do.
Eat, greet and pass things with your right hand, and accept at least one glass of mint tea when it's offered — refusing outright can seem cold.

neighborhoods.name: Medina
neighborhoods.blurb: The walled old city, a UNESCO-listed maze of souks, riads, mosques and workshops radiating out from Jemaa el-Fnaa. Stay here for full immersion.

neighborhoods.name: Kasbah
neighborhoods.blurb: The southern quarter around the Saadian Tombs and El Badi Palace, a notch calmer than the northern souks, with rooftop cafés and easy taxi access.

neighborhoods.name: Gueliz
neighborhoods.blurb: The French-built new town, with wide boulevards, galleries, boutiques, wine bars and the city's best international restaurants.

neighborhoods.name: Hivernage
neighborhoods.blurb: An upscale garden district between the medina and Gueliz, home to luxury hotels, nightclubs and palm-lined avenues.

neighborhoods.name: Palmeraie
neighborhoods.blurb: A vast palm oasis on the northern edge of the city dotted with resort hotels, villas, golf courses and camel-ride stables — a peaceful escape from the medina bustle.

dishes.name: Tanjia marrakchia
dishes.description: Marrakech's 'bachelor's stew': beef or lamb with preserved lemon, garlic, cumin and saffron, sealed in a clay urn and slow-cooked for hours in the embers of a hammam furnace.

dishes.name: Chicken tagine with preserved lemon
dishes.description: The classic conical-pot stew, meltingly tender and perfumed with ginger, saffron, green olives and salty lemon rind, mopped up with round khobz bread.

dishes.name: Harira
dishes.description: A hearty tomato, lentil and chickpea soup with fresh herbs and a squeeze of lemon, famous for breaking the Ramadan fast but eaten all year.

dishes.name: Msemen
dishes.description: Flaky square griddle pancakes folded from buttery layers, eaten at breakfast with honey or amlou, a paste of argan oil, almonds and honey.

dishes.name: Atay (mint tea)
dishes.description: Green tea brewed with fistfuls of fresh spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from a height to raise a foam — the ritual at the heart of Moroccan hospitality.

events.name: Marrakech Marathon
events.description: Runners loop past the medina walls, palm groves and boulevards in one of Africa's flattest and most scenic city marathons.

events.name: 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair
events.description: The Marrakech edition of this leading fair brings galleries and artists from across Africa and its diaspora to the city, with satellite exhibitions around town.

events.name: Festival National des Arts Populaires
events.description: Folk troupes from every corner of Morocco — acrobats, Gnawa musicians, Amazigh dancers — perform in historic venues across the city.

events.name: Marrakech International Film Festival
events.description: Stars and directors gather for premieres and galas, while free open-air screenings in Jemaa el-Fnaa bring cinema to everyone.

attractions.name: Jemaa el-Fnaa
attractions.description: By day the great square hosts orange-juice carts, henna artists and snake charmers; by dusk it morphs into a smoky open-air food court and a stage for storytellers, Gnawa musicians and acrobats. Watch the spectacle unfold from a rooftop café, then dive in.
attractions.bookingTip: Agree prices before sitting down at the grill stalls, send back anything you didn't order, and keep small change for performers you photograph.

attractions.name: Koutoubia Mosque
attractions.description: The 12th-century minaret of Marrakech's largest mosque soars 77 metres over the medina, a masterpiece of Almohad design and a sister to Seville's Giralda. Non-Muslims can't enter, but the rose gardens alongside are lovely at sunset as the call to prayer rings out.
attractions.hours: Exterior and gardens open daily; interior for Muslim worshippers only
attractions.bookingTip: Come around sunset for the best light on the minaret, then stroll five minutes to Jemaa el-Fnaa as it comes alive.

attractions.name: Bahia Palace
attractions.description: Built in the late 19th century for a powerful grand vizier, this rambling palace is a feast of painted cedar ceilings, zellige mosaics and courtyards shaded by orange trees. Its name means 'brilliance', and the detail lives up to it.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive at 09:00 before tour groups fill the courtyards — and remember to look up, as the ceilings are the highlight.

attractions.name: Majorelle Garden
attractions.description: Created by painter Jacques Majorelle and later rescued by Yves Saint Laurent, this garden pairs giant cacti, bamboo groves and lily ponds with a villa painted the electric cobalt now known as Majorelle blue. The Berber arts museum inside and the nearby YSL museum make a perfect cultural pairing.
attractions.bookingTip: Book a timed ticket online in advance and pick the first slot to enjoy the paths before the crowds.

attractions.name: Ben Youssef Madrasa
attractions.description: Once among the largest Quranic schools in North Africa, this 16th-century madrasa centres on a courtyard of breathtaking symmetry: carved cedar, stucco lacework and zellige wrapped around a still reflecting pool. Climb upstairs to peek into the tiny cells where students once lived.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive right at opening to photograph the courtyard pool without a crowd reflected in it.

attractions.name: Saadian Tombs
attractions.description: Walled off for centuries and only rediscovered in the early 20th century, this royal necropolis shelters the tombs of Saadian sultans beneath honeycombed muqarnas domes and Italian marble columns. The Hall of Twelve Columns is one of Morocco's most exquisite rooms.
attractions.bookingTip: A queue forms for the single viewing spot at the main chamber, so go first thing or late in the afternoon.

attractions.name: El Badi Palace
attractions.description: Once lavished with gold, onyx and Italian marble, this 16th-century palace was stripped bare a century later, leaving vast ruined courtyards, sunken orange gardens and ramparts where storks nest. Climb to the terrace for sweeping views over the medina to the Atlas.
attractions.bookingTip: Don't miss the pavilion displaying the Koutoubia's carved medieval minbar, a woodworking masterpiece.

attractions.name: Mellah
attractions.description: Marrakech's historic Jewish quarter, founded in the 16th century, is a tangle of lanes with a spice square, jewellers and the restored Lazama Synagogue. The walled Jewish cemetery, with thousands of whitewashed tombs, is haunting and deeply peaceful.
attractions.hours: Lanes open daily; synagogue and cemetery closed Saturdays and Jewish holidays
attractions.bookingTip: Hire a licensed guide for context — the quarter's layered history is easy to miss alone, and a guide deflects the fake ones.

attractions.name: Dar Si Said
attractions.description: A 19th-century mansion reborn as a museum of weaving and carpets, with painted ceilings and courtyards framing centuries-old Amazigh rugs, textiles and costumes. It's cool, quiet and a smart primer before you tackle the carpet souk.
attractions.bookingTip: Visit before carpet shopping — learning the regional styles and natural dyes will help you spot quality and haggle with confidence.

attractions.name: Ourika Valley
attractions.description: About an hour south of the city, the Ourika River carves a green ribbon through the High Atlas foothills, lined with Berber villages, walnut groves and cafés with tables set right in the water. Hike up to the Setti Fatma waterfalls for a proper taste of the mountains.
attractions.hours: Accessible year-round; best during daylight hours
attractions.bookingTip: Avoid Sundays, when day-trippers from the city pack the valley, and hire a local guide for the scramble to the upper falls.

hotels.name: Palais Qamar Lahmar
hotels.description: A palace-style hotel of carved plaster, cedar doors and tiled pools set in walled gardens of olive and orange trees, with the Koutoubia minaret rising beyond the palms. Its marble hammam and spa rank among the city's finest.

hotels.name: Riad Tbourida
hotels.description: Seven rooms arranged around a courtyard plunge pool and a lemon tree, with tadelakt bathrooms and textiles woven by Atlas cooperatives. The rooftop breakfast of msemen and amlou comes with the call to prayer drifting over the medina.

hotels.name: Hostel Sfenj Social
hotels.description: A cheerful hostel two minutes from the main square, with bunk rooms around a tiled courtyard, a rooftop hangout strung with hammocks and nightly family-style tagine dinners. Staff lead free medina orientation walks every morning.

hotels.name: Studio Tadelakt Hotel
hotels.description: Polished tadelakt walls, terracotta and ochre tones and contemporary Moroccan art give this Gueliz hotel a sleek, sun-baked look. The rooftop pool bar gazes towards the Atlas on clear days.

hotels.name: Dar Khettara
hotels.description: A restored 19th-century merchant's house near the Kasbah mosque, keeping its painted cedar ceilings, fountain courtyard and original zellige floors. The owners' family has lived in the Kasbah for generations and shares insider routes through the souks.

hotels.name: Kasbah Assif Lodge
hotels.description: An earth-walled lodge terraced into the hillside above the Ourika River, with an infinity pool facing snow-capped peaks and a vegetable garden supplying the kitchen. Guided walks to Berber villages and waterfalls leave from the front door.

restaurants.name: Chez Mbarka Harira Stall
restaurants.description: A family-run stall in the square's evening food court, where Mbarka's daughters ladle harira and spiced lentils alongside sizzling merguez and fried fish. Plastic benches, paper napkins and one of the best-value dinners in town.

restaurants.name: Café Nous-Nous du Mellah
restaurants.description: A sunny corner café by the spice square where locals linger over nous-nous — half coffee, half milk — and warm msemen with honey. The upstairs terrace overlooks the storks nesting on El Badi's walls.

restaurants.name: Laqlaq Rooftop Tasting Room
restaurants.description: A candlelit rooftop named for the storks nesting on the palace walls next door, serving a seven-course journey through Morocco's regions, from Fez-style pastilla to Saharan spiced lamb. It's licensed, with Moroccan wine pairings or an inventive alcohol-free flight.
restaurants.signatureDish: Pigeon pastilla with cinnamon and almonds

restaurants.name: Tanjia Chez Moulay Brahim
restaurants.description: Clay urns of beef, preserved lemon and cumin are sealed each morning and sent to the neighbourhood hammam furnace, returning at lunchtime as tender, garlicky tanjia. Eat it with bread at shared tables near the Kasbah mosque.

restaurants.name: Stah Koutoubia
restaurants.description: A breezy roof terrace with front-row views of the Koutoubia minaret, serving tagines, couscous and grilled kefta with fresh-squeezed juices and mint tea. Sunset tables are the hottest seats in the medina.
restaurants.signatureDish: Chicken tagine with preserved lemon and olives

restaurants.name: Pastificio Ocra
restaurants.description: When you need a break from tagine, this Gueliz trattoria rolls fresh pasta daily and serves it in a leafy courtyard. Pair it with a glass of Moroccan gris wine from the Meknes vineyards.

restaurants.name: Café Henna Verte
restaurants.description: A tranquil riad courtyard serving plant-based riffs on Moroccan classics — seven-vegetable couscous, lentil briouats and beetroot zaalouk — plus fresh juices and fragrant teas. A calm refuge after the souks.

restaurants.name: Assif Riverside Tagines
restaurants.description: Low tables set right in the shallows of the Ourika River, where you cool your feet in snowmelt while a clay tagine bubbles on a charcoal brazier beside you. Flatbread arrives hot from a clay oven.
restaurants.signatureDish: Berber tagine of lamb and seasonal vegetables

experiences.name: Souk-to-Tagine Cooking Class in a Medina Riad
experiences.description: Shop for spices, vegetables and preserved lemons with a dada, a traditional Moroccan cook, then return to her riad kitchen to make zaalouk, a chicken tagine and fresh bread. Lunch is served on the terrace with mint tea poured the proper way.

experiences.name: Jemaa el-Fnaa After-Dark Street-Food Walk
experiences.description: Graze through the square's smoky grill stalls and the food alleys behind it with a local foodie who knows which vendors locals trust — from slow-roasted mechoui lamb to snail broth and sugar-dusted sfenj doughnuts. Finish with mint tea on a rooftop above the chaos.

experiences.name: Traditional Hammam and Argan Oil Ritual
experiences.description: Steam in a domed, candlelit hammam before an attendant scrubs you down with black olive soap and a kessa glove, followed by a rhassoul clay wrap and an argan oil massage. You'll emerge softer than you thought possible.

experiences.name: High Atlas Villages and Ourika Waterfalls Day Trip
experiences.description: Swap the city for the Ourika Valley, stopping at a women's argan-oil cooperative and a Berber family home for tea before hiking to the Setti Fatma waterfalls with a mountain guide. Lunch is a tagine at a riverside café.
